description.narrative: Escalation of violence in Gaza has left a significant number of civilians killed <(>&<)> wounded, with over 330K displaced. The violence has damaged shelters <(>&<)> infrastructure. The situation is becoming increasingly dire. Even before Oct-23, over 80% of Gazans needed humanitarian aid. Because of politically driven pressure, some donors have stopped/cut aid, creating severe service gaps. With the complete seize imposed, ppl. are struggling to secure cash to support their basic needs to buy food, water <(>&<)> medicine. Thousands have lost their homes and are now forced into temporary shelters, facing multiple protection risks. Shutdown of Gaza's power plant due to lack of fuel <(>&<)> hundreds of Israeli military airstrikes have destroyed essential WASH infrastructures <(>&<)>public services. This raises fears that Gaza will run out of electricity <(>&<)> water imminently. The WASH sector faces multiple challenges, including access and distribution of materials and items necessary for WASH facilities. Israel's decision to cut water supply and electricity has impacted 5 WASH infrastructures <(>&<)> facilities, which served over 600K people. Gaza's current electricity generation is less than 60 MW, falling significantly short of the necessary power to sustain WASH services across the entire Gaza. Against this backdrop Oxfam and local partners PEF, AISHA <(>&<)> CMWU propose to assist 18K people in Gaza city <(>&<)> North Gaza, with WASH <(>&<)> protection assistance incl. repair of damaged WASH networks aligning with Cluster response prioritization and Oxfam's expertise, distribute Hygiene Kit E-vouchers, including menstrual hygiene items <(>&<)> mitigating protection related risks, by supporting women and children whose needs are deprioritized in crises. Needs have been discussed with JR partners in Gaza to identify complementary activities and avoid duplication. Oxfam is well-positioned to respond with a well-established WASH program, focusing on strategic interventions in water systems <(>&<)> infrastructure for long-term impact

participating-org.narrative:
Oxfam Novib has been active in the Occupied Palestinian Territory/Israel (OPT/I) since 1982 and working with Palestinian refugees in Lebanon since the mid 1980s. It has built up a strong network of relationships with local NGOs and counts among its localcounterparts some of the largest and most professional NGOs in various sectors. It has accompanied these NGOs in their development from ad hoc volunteer groups to sizeable professional institutions with national outreach. At the same time the conceptualisation of the programme has evolved from three country programs in the early 1990s to a program for Palestinians in the Middle East (PME) working withPalestinians in OPT, Israel and Lebanon.
The programme has changed over the years with the establishment of the Palestinian Authority (PA) in the mid-1990s from a focus on support and service provision at a grassroots level and grassroots mobilization, to working towards influencing the establishment of the PA, its lawmaking and supporting building a democratic state # this involved supporting efforts of Palestinian civil society to build the basis for a democratic Palestinian state with room for civil participation, ensuring inclusion of vulnerable groups, refugees and women, and shaping its laws and systems. Oxfam Novib has also supported partners that are working on the provision of humanitarian assistance, response preparedness and conflict transformation. We have also supported partners in the provision of health services, access to quality education and gender justice.

comment.narrative: It was planned to repair & maintenance of 5 sewage networks to mitigate public health threats in line with the SPHERE standards. However, the repair and rehabilitation of a larger number of damaged public wastewater networks in Gaza, exceeding the original plan, were achieved through several key factors. The Coastal Municipalities Water Utility (CMWU) effectively utilized available materials from its warehouses or secured from donors other than Oxfam, significantly reducing maintenance costs and enablingthe execution of five separate contracts with local contractors throughout the project. Additionally, in agreement with the donor, funds initially allocated for purchasing materials from outside Gaza were reallocated to cover additional repair costs due to challenges in coordinating the entry of materials into Gaza. This adjustment allowed the use of locally available resources through contractor agreements. Furthermore, interventions were prioritized based on ongoing needs assessments by CMWU, Oxfam, and the PEF, targeting densely populated areas with high numbers of displaced persons and residents. These combined efforts expanded the project's scope, reaching a larger number of affected individuals and enhancing its overall impact.
